response_text:
## What the table shows

This is a worked example from NCHS (National Center for Health Statistics), using 2013–2014 NHANES data on children aged 8–17. Its real subject isn't blood pressure — it's **when a survey estimate is solid enough to publish**.

**The estimates for elevated blood pressure:**

| Group | Kids surveyed | Estimate | Range it could plausibly be |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-Hispanic white | 460 | 0.5% | 0.1% – 1.6% |
| Non-Hispanic Black | 447 | 2.0% | 0.3% – 6.4% |
| Non-Hispanic Asian | 164 | 0.9% | 0.0% – 5.1% |
| Hispanic | 589 | 2.5% | 1.4% – 4.1% |

Elevated blood pressure is rare in children — roughly 1 in 50 or fewer in every group. But rare outcomes are exactly the ones that are hardest to measure: only a handful of kids in each sample actually had it, so the estimates wobble.

## The point being illustrated

NCHS judges reliability two ways, and the example is built to show that they disagree:

**The old way (relative standard error).** Measure the error *as a share of the estimate itself*. When the estimate is tiny, almost any error looks huge in relative terms. The white estimate has an RSE of 58% — well past the 30% cutoff — so this rule would have thrown it out, even though the estimate is pinned down to a range barely 1.5 percentage points wide. That's the flaw: it punishes an estimate for being small, not for being imprecise.

**The current way (confidence interval width).** Ask instead how *wide* the plausible range is, in actual percentage points:

- **Narrow range → publish.** White (1.6 points) and Hispanic (2.7 points) are both tight enough to be useful. Both get published.
- **Wider range → look closer.** Black (6.1 points) and Asian (5.1 points) are wide enough to warrant a second check — is the range wide compared to the estimate? For Black children, the range is 3 times the size of the estimate; for Asian children, more than 5 times. Both blow past the 130% limit, so **both are suppressed.** "2.0%" and "0.9%" aren't reported, because the data can't distinguish them from "nearly zero" or "several times higher."

Other checks all passed for every group: each had at least one child with elevated blood pressure but not all of them, and each had enough degrees of freedom (more than 8) for the statistics to behave.

## The mirror-image wrinkle

Every row has a flip side: the share with *normal or borderline* blood pressure (99.5%, 98.0%, 99.1%, 97.5%). These carry exactly the same uncertainty — the range for Black children is still 6.1 percentage points wide — but now that width sits next to a number near 100 instead of near 2. As a fraction of the estimate it's about 6%, comfortably under the limit.

So the same underlying data gets published one way and suppressed the other. NCHS handles this honestly rather than quietly: the "normal or borderline" figures are printed **with a footnote saying their complement didn't meet the standard.** Readers who want to subtract from 100 to recover the suppressed number are warned that the number wasn't trustworthy enough to print.

## The takeaway

A percentage on its own says nothing about whether it can be trusted. Small samples, split into subgroups, measuring a rare condition, produce numbers that look specific but aren't. These rules decide what gets published, what gets flagged, and what gets withheld — and the white-children row is the whole argument in miniature: under the old rule it vanishes, under the current one it's perfectly publishable.
